questions.question: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[X]^2[Y]. In an experiment with [X] = 0.10 mol dm^-3 and [Y] = 0.20 mol dm^-3, the initial rate is 4.0 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3 s^-1. What is the value of k, with its units? A 2.0 x 10^-2 dm^3 mol^-1 s^-1, B 0.10 dm^6 mol^-2 s^-1, C 0.20 dm^3 mol^-1 s^-1, D 0.20 dm^6 mol^-2 s^-1.
steps: Units: mol dm^-3 s^-1 / (mol^3 dm^-9) = dm^6 mol^-2 s^-1 for a third order reaction.
A treats the reaction as second order; B squares [Y] instead of [X]; C has the right value but the units of a second order reaction.

questions.question: A first order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0231 min^-1. What is the half-life of the reaction? A 0.0333 min, B 30.0 min, C 43.3 min, D 15.0 min.
steps: For a first order reaction, t(1/2) = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / 0.0231 = 30.0 min.
A is k / ln 2, C is 1 / k, D is half of the correct value.

questions.question: The rate of a reaction approximately doubles when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 310 K. Explain, with reference to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, why a small rise in temperature has such a large effect on the rate.
questions.answer: At higher temperature many more molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so many more collisions are successful
steps: At the higher temperature the distribution curve shifts to higher energy (the peak is lower and further right); the area under the curve is unchanged because the number of molecules is the same
The high-energy tail rises sharply, so the proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy increases by a large factor (the activation energy itself is unchanged)
A much greater fraction of collisions is successful, so the rate increases (here it roughly doubles)
accept: Molecules also have a higher mean kinetic energy, move faster and collide more often, but this is a much smaller effect than the change in the fraction with enough energy
The activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful
The area under the curve to the right of the activation energy is much larger at the higher temperature
The fraction of molecules with energy of at least the activation energy depends exponentially on temperature

questions.question: The hydrolysis of an organic compound X is first order with respect to X. The half-life is 25.0 minutes at 330 K. Calculate the rate constant in min^-1, and the time taken for the concentration of X to fall from 0.800 mol dm^-3 to 0.100 mol dm^-3 at this temperature.
steps: Time = 3 x 25.0 = 75.0 min (1 mark).

questions.question: Nitrogen dioxide reacts with carbon monoxide: NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g). Three experiments at the same temperature gave these initial rates. Experiment 1: [NO2] = 0.0100 mol dm^-3, [CO] = 0.0200 mol dm^-3, rate = 5.0 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3 s^-1. Experiment 2: [NO2] = 0.0100 mol dm^-3, [CO] = 0.0400 mol dm^-3, rate = 5.0 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3 s^-1. Experiment 3: [NO2] = 0.0200 mol dm^-3, [CO] = 0.0200 mol dm^-3, rate = 2.0 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3 s^-1. Determine the order of reaction with respect to NO2 and with respect to CO, showing your reasoning.
questions.answer: Second order with respect to NO2; zero order with respect to CO
steps: Experiments 1 and 2: [CO] doubles, [NO2] is constant and the rate is unchanged, so the order with respect to CO is zero
Experiments 1 and 3: [NO2] doubles, [CO] is constant and the rate increases by a factor of 4 (2.0 x 10^-4 / 5.0 x 10^-5)
The rate is proportional to [NO2]^2 (2^2 = 4), so the order with respect to NO2 is 2
accept: Rate is independent of [CO]
Overall order of the reaction is 2
Each order is found by changing one concentration at a time and keeping the other concentration constant

questions.question: The reaction NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g) is second order with respect to NO2 and zero order with respect to CO. Write the rate equation for the reaction.
steps: A reactant that is zero order does not appear in the rate equation, so [CO] is left out.
The rate equation is rate = k[NO2]^2.

questions.question: For the reaction NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g), rate = k[NO2]^2. In Experiment 1 the initial rate is 5.0 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3 s^-1 when [NO2] = 0.0100 mol dm^-3. Calculate the value of k and state its units.
steps: Units: mol dm^-3 s^-1 / mol^2 dm^-6 = dm^3 mol^-1 s^-1 (1 mark).

questions.question: A mechanism for NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g) is: step 1, NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO (slow); step 2, NO3 + CO -> NO2 + CO2 (fast). The rate equation is rate = k[NO2]^2. Show that the two steps add up to the overall equation, and explain how the mechanism is consistent with the rate equation.
questions.answer: The steps add to give NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2; the slow step 1 involves two NO2 and no CO, so rate = k[NO2]^2
steps: Adding the steps: 2NO2 + NO3 + CO -> NO3 + NO + NO2 + CO2; cancelling NO3 and one NO2 gives NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2
Step 1 is the slow, rate-determining step and it involves two NO2 molecules, so the rate depends on [NO2]^2
CO takes part only in the fast step after the rate-determining step, so the rate does not depend on [CO] (zero order)
accept: NO3 is an intermediate: it is formed in step 1 and used up in step 2, so it does not appear in the overall equation
The rate equation contains only the species that react in the rate-determining step (and anything before it)
The powers in the rate equation match the number of molecules of each species in the slow step

questions.question: The rate constant for a first order reaction is 3.20 x 10^-5 s^-1 at 298 K and 5.50 x 10^-4 s^-1 at 318 K. Use the Arrhenius equation, ln k = -Ea/(RT) + constant, to calculate the activation energy in kJ mol^-1. R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1.
steps: Subtracting the equations at the two temperatures: ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 - 1/T2) (1 mark).
Ea = +112 kJ mol^-1 (1 mark).

questions.question: Explain, with reference to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction at constant temperature.
questions.answer: The catalyst gives an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so more molecules have enough energy to react
steps: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway (mechanism)
This pathway has a lower activation energy
The temperature is unchanged, so the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies is unchanged
A greater proportion of molecules has energy equal to or greater than the new, lower activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second and the rate increases
accept: The activation energy is shown on the energy axis further to the left, so the area under the curve to the right of it is larger
The total area under the curve (the number of molecules) is the same
A heterogeneous catalyst provides a surface on which reactants adsorb, weakening bonds
The catalyst is not used up and does not change the position of equilibrium

questions.question: The reaction CH3COCH3(aq) + I2(aq) -> CH3COCH2I(aq) + HI(aq) is catalysed by acid. Iodine solution is brown and the other substances in the mixture are colourless. Suggest why colorimetry is a suitable method for following the rate of this reaction.
questions.answer: Iodine is the only coloured substance, so absorbance is proportional to [I2] and can be followed continuously without taking samples
steps: Iodine is the only coloured species, so the absorbance of the mixture is proportional to the concentration of iodine
The absorbance decreases as iodine is used up and can be measured continuously, without removing samples or stopping the reaction
accept: A calibration curve of absorbance against iodine concentration converts the readings to concentrations
A colorimeter with a suitable filter (blue or violet for brown iodine) is used
A graph of [I2] against time gives the rate from the gradient

questions.question: Which is the expression for Kp for the equilibrium C(s) + CO2(g) <=> 2CO(g)? A Kp = p(CO)^2 / p(CO2), B Kp = p(CO)^2 / (p(C) x p(CO2)), C Kp = 2p(CO) / p(CO2), D Kp = p(CO2) / p(CO)^2.
steps: Solids do not appear in the expression for Kp because they have no partial pressure, so p(C) is omitted.
The coefficient 2 becomes a power: p(CO)^2.
B includes carbon, C multiplies p(CO) by 2 instead of squaring it, and D is inverted.

questions.question: The equilibrium N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g) has Delta H = +57 kJ mol^-1. Which change increases both the equilibrium yield of NO2 and the value of Kp? A increasing the total pressure at constant temperature, B adding a catalyst, C increasing the temperature, D removing NO2 as it forms.
steps: Kp changes only with temperature. The forward reaction is endothermic, so raising the temperature moves the equilibrium to the right and increases Kp.
A moves the equilibrium to the left (fewer moles of gas) and leaves Kp unchanged; B has no effect on yield or Kp; D increases the yield but Kp is unchanged.

questions.question: 0.250 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.350 mol of ethanol were mixed with a catalyst and left to reach equilibrium: CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. The equilibrium mixture contained 0.190 mol of ethyl ethanoate. Calculate the value of Kc.
steps: Equilibrium moles: ethanoic acid = 0.250 - 0.190 = 0.060; ethanol = 0.350 - 0.190 = 0.160; water = 0.190 (1 mark).
Kc = [CH3COOC2H5][H2O] / ([CH3COOH][C2H5OH]) (1 mark).
There are equal numbers of moles of reactants and products, so the volume cancels and moles can be used: Kc = (0.190 x 0.190) / (0.060 x 0.160) = 3.76, with no units (1 mark).

questions.question: Dinitrogen tetraoxide dissociates: N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g). Write the expression for Kp for this equilibrium.
steps: Kp is the product of the partial pressures of the products, each raised to the power of its coefficient, divided by the same for the reactants.
Kp = p(NO2)^2 / p(N2O4).

questions.question: 1.00 mol of N2O4(g) is placed in a vessel and allowed to dissociate: N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g). At equilibrium at 350 K the total pressure is 200 kPa and 30.0% of the N2O4 has dissociated. Calculate the partial pressures of N2O4 and NO2 at equilibrium.
steps: Moles dissociated = 0.300, so at equilibrium n(N2O4) = 0.700 mol and n(NO2) = 2 x 0.300 = 0.600 mol; total = 1.300 mol (1 mark).
Partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure: p(N2O4) = (0.700 / 1.300) x 200 = 107.7 kPa; p(NO2) = (0.600 / 1.300) x 200 = 92.3 kPa (1 mark).

questions.question: For N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g) at 350 K, the equilibrium partial pressures are p(N2O4) = 107.7 kPa and p(NO2) = 92.3 kPa. Calculate Kp, including units.
steps: Units: kPa^2 / kPa = kPa (1 mark).

questions.question: The equilibrium N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g) at 350 K is compressed so that the total pressure is doubled from 200 kPa to 400 kPa, at constant temperature. State and explain the effect on the value of Kp and on the percentage of N2O4 that has dissociated.
questions.answer: Kp is unchanged; the percentage dissociation decreases because the equilibrium shifts towards N2O4, the side with fewer moles of gas
steps: Kp is unchanged because it depends only on temperature
The equilibrium shifts to the left, the side with fewer moles of gas (1 mol N2O4 against 2 mol NO2), to reduce the increase in pressure
So less N2O4 is dissociated, and the proportion of NO2 in the mixture falls
accept: Kp does not depend on pressure or on the position of equilibrium
The partial pressure of NO2 falls in proportion to the partial pressure of N2O4, so the ratio p(NO2)^2 / p(N2O4) returns to the same value as before
Le Chatelier: the system opposes the increase in pressure by reducing the number of moles of gas

questions.question: State what is meant by the term dynamic equilibrium.
questions.answer: The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate in a closed system, so the concentrations stay constant
steps: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
Both reactions are still taking place, but in a closed system the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant
accept: No reactants or products enter or leave the system (closed system)
Reactant molecules continue to change into product molecules and product molecules into reactant molecules
Macroscopic properties such as colour or pressure stay constant

questions.question: Sulfur trioxide is made in the Contact process: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), Delta H = -197 kJ mol^-1. The reaction is carried out at about 450 C and a pressure of 100 to 200 kPa, using a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst. Explain why these conditions are used, with reference to the equilibrium yield, the rate of reaction and the cost.
questions.answer: Compromise conditions: moderate temperature and low pressure give a high enough yield at a good rate, and the catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield
steps: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield
But a low temperature makes the rate too slow, so 450 C is a compromise that gives an acceptable rate and a high yield
There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so a high pressure would increase the yield
The yield is already high at 100 to 200 kPa, so a high pressure is not worth the extra cost of equipment and energy, or the safety risks
The catalyst provides a route with a lower activation energy, so the reaction is fast enough at a moderate temperature (saving energy cost)
The catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield, only the time taken to reach equilibrium
accept: A higher temperature would favour the endothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium would move to the left and the yield would fall
A higher temperature increases the rate because a greater proportion of molecules has energy of at least the activation energy
High pressure needs thick-walled pipes and compressors, which are expensive to build and run
The catalyst is not used up, so it can be reused, which keeps costs down

questions.question: The equilibrium constant, Kp, for CO(g) + 2H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g) decreases when the temperature is raised from 500 K to 600 K. Deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and explain your answer.
questions.answer: Exothermic: the equilibrium moves left when the temperature is raised, so the reverse reaction is endothermic
steps: Kp falls, so the position of equilibrium moves to the left when the temperature is raised
A rise in temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the reverse reaction is endothermic and the forward reaction is exothermic
accept: The equilibrium yield of CH3OH decreases as the temperature rises
Delta H for the forward reaction is negative
By Le Chatelier, the system opposes the rise in temperature by absorbing heat in the endothermic direction

questions.question: What is the pH of 0.0250 mol dm^-3 barium hydroxide solution at 298 K? Kw = 1.00 x 10^-14 mol^2 dm^-6. A 1.30, B 12.70, C 12.40, D 1.60.
steps: Ba(OH)2 releases 2 mol of OH- per mole, so [OH-] = 2 x 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol dm^-3.
A is pOH; C uses [OH-] = 0.0250; D is -log 0.0250.

questions.question: What is the pH of 0.100 mol dm^-3 ethanoic acid? Ka for ethanoic acid = 1.74 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3. A 1.00, B 4.76, C 2.88, D 5.76.
steps: Ka = [H+]^2 / [CH3COOH], so [H+] = sqrt(Ka x c) = sqrt(1.74 x 10^-5 x 0.100) = 1.32 x 10^-3 mol dm^-3.
A assumes the acid is strong; B is the pKa; D comes from using [H+] = Ka x c instead of the square root.

questions.question: A buffer solution is made by adding 20.0 cm^3 of 0.150 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution to 50.0 cm^3 of 0.200 mol dm^-3 ethanoic acid. Calculate the pH of the buffer. Ka for ethanoic acid = 1.74 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3.
steps: Moles of CH3COOH at the start = 0.0500 x 0.200 = 0.0100 mol; moles of NaOH = 0.0200 x 0.150 = 0.00300 mol (1 mark).
After reaction: CH3COOH = 0.0100 - 0.00300 = 0.00700 mol and CH3COO- = 0.00300 mol (1 mark).
Ka = [H+][CH3COO-] / [CH3COOH], so [H+] = Ka x 0.00700 / 0.00300 = 4.06 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3; the volume cancels in the ratio (1 mark).

questions.question: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, is a weak acid. Write the expression for its acid dissociation constant, Ka.
steps: The equilibrium is HCOOH <=> H+ + HCOO-.
Ka = [H+][HCOO-] / [HCOOH].

questions.question: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.100 mol dm^-3 methanoic acid, HCOOH, is to be titrated with 0.100 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution. Calculate the pH of the methanoic acid before any sodium hydroxide is added. Ka for methanoic acid = 1.78 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3.
steps: Ka = [H+]^2 / [HCOOH], assuming [H+] = [HCOO-] and that [HCOOH] is unchanged (1 mark).

questions.question: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.100 mol dm^-3 methanoic acid, HCOOH, is titrated with 0.100 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution. Calculate the pH of the mixture after 10.0 cm^3 of sodium hydroxide solution has been added. Ka for methanoic acid = 1.78 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3.
steps: Moles of HCOOH at the start = 0.0250 x 0.100 = 0.00250 mol; moles of NaOH added = 0.0100 x 0.100 = 0.00100 mol (1 mark).
After reaction: HCOOH = 0.00150 mol and HCOO- = 0.00100 mol (1 mark).

questions.question: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.100 mol dm^-3 methanoic acid is titrated with 0.100 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution. Determine the volume of sodium hydroxide solution at the equivalence point, and choose the most suitable indicator from methyl orange (pH range 3.1 to 4.4), bromothymol blue (pH range 6.0 to 7.6) and phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3 to 10.0). The pH at the equivalence point is above 7.
steps: HCOOH and NaOH react 1 : 1 and the concentrations are equal, so the equivalence point is at 0.0250 x 0.100 / 0.100 = 25.0 cm^3
The salt formed, sodium methanoate, makes the solution alkaline at equivalence, so the indicator must change colour in the alkaline range: phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3 to 10.0)
accept: Methyl orange and bromothymol blue change colour at lower pH, before the equivalence point, so they would give a titre that is too small
The methanoate ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid: HCOO- + H2O <=> HCOOH + OH-
Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at the end point

questions.question: 30.0 cm^3 of 0.150 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid is added to 20.0 cm^3 of 0.100 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution. Calculate the pH of the mixture.
A 0.0500 mol dm^-3 solution of a weak monobasic acid, HX, has a pH of 3.40. Calculate the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of HX and state its units.
steps: Ka = 3.17 x 10^-6 mol dm^-3 (1 mark).

questions.question: State two assumptions made when calculating the acid dissociation constant of a weak acid HX from the pH of its solution.
questions.answer: [H+] = [X-] (all H+ comes from the acid); [HX] at equilibrium is the same as the initial concentration
steps: The ionisation of water makes a negligible contribution to [H+], so [H+] = [X-]
The acid is only slightly dissociated, so the equilibrium concentration of HX is approximately equal to its initial concentration
accept: All the H+ ions come from the dissociation of HX
Dissociation of HX is small, so [HX]equilibrium = [HX]initial
The temperature is constant, so Ka is constant

questions.question: The acid dissociation constant of a weak acid HX is 3.17 x 10^-6 mol dm^-3. Calculate its pKa.
steps: pKa = -log10(Ka).

questions.question: The pH of human blood is kept close to 7.4 by a buffer system containing carbonic acid, H2CO3, and hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO3-. Explain how this buffer limits the change in pH when lactic acid enters the blood during exercise, and when a small amount of alkali enters the blood.
questions.answer: Added H+ reacts with HCO3-, shifting the equilibrium to H2CO3; added OH- reacts with H+ and H2CO3 dissociates to replace it
steps: The equilibrium is H2CO3 <=> H+ + HCO3-; the blood contains large amounts of both the weak acid H2CO3 and its conjugate base HCO3-
When lactic acid is added, the extra H+ reacts with HCO3-: H+ + HCO3- -> H2CO3, so the equilibrium moves to the left
The concentration of HCO3- is large compared with the amount of H+ added, so the ratio [H2CO3] / [HCO3-] changes only slightly and the pH stays almost constant
When alkali is added, OH- reacts with H+: H+ + OH- -> H2O
More H2CO3 dissociates to replace the H+ removed (the equilibrium moves to the right), so the ratio changes little and the pH changes only slightly
accept: [H+] = Ka x [H2CO3] / [HCO3-], so the pH depends on the ratio of the two concentrations, which changes very little
Added OH- may be shown reacting directly with H2CO3: OH- + H2CO3 -> HCO3- + H2O
The buffer is effective because the weak acid and its conjugate base are both present in large amounts
Le Chatelier: the equilibrium moves to oppose each change

questions.question: Which pair of aqueous solutions gives a precipitate when mixed? A magnesium sulfate and barium chloride, B sodium nitrate and potassium chloride, C calcium nitrate and sodium chloride, D ammonium sulfate and potassium nitrate.
questions.answer: A: magnesium sulfate and barium chloride
steps: Barium sulfate is insoluble: Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s), so a white precipitate forms in A.
All the nitrates, and the chlorides, ammonium salts and potassium salts in B, C and D, are soluble, so no precipitate forms.

questions.question: A salt dissolves in water with an enthalpy change of solution of +12 kJ mol^-1 and an entropy change of the system of +110 J K^-1 mol^-1 at 298 K. Which statement is correct? A The salt cannot dissolve because the process is endothermic, B The entropy change of the surroundings is +40.3 J K^-1 mol^-1, C The total entropy change is -40.3 J K^-1 mol^-1, so dissolving is not feasible, D The total entropy change is +69.7 J K^-1 mol^-1, so dissolving is feasible.
questions.answer: D: the total entropy change is +69.7 J K^-1 mol^-1, so dissolving is feasible
steps: Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T = -12 000 / 298 = -40.3 J K^-1 mol^-1 (the process is endothermic).
Delta S total = +110 + (-40.3) = +69.7 J K^-1 mol^-1; a positive total means that dissolving is feasible.
A ignores the entropy increase of the system; B has the wrong sign for Delta S surroundings; C ignores Delta S system.

questions.question: A student determines the solubility of barium hydroxide by titrating a saturated solution with hydrochloric acid. Write the equation for the reaction between barium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid.
steps: Barium hydroxide has two hydroxide ions per formula unit, so it neutralises 2 mol of HCl per mole.
Ba(OH)2 + 2HCl -> BaCl2 + 2H2O.

questions.question: 25.0 cm^3 of a saturated solution of barium hydroxide at 293 K was diluted to 250.0 cm^3 in a volumetric flask. A 25.0 cm^3 portion of the diluted solution needed a mean titre of 11.30 cm^3 of 0.100 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid for neutralisation: Ba(OH)2 + 2HCl -> BaCl2 + 2H2O. Calculate the concentration of barium hydroxide in the diluted solution, in mol dm^-3.
steps: Moles of HCl = 0.01130 x 0.100 = 1.13 x 10^-3 mol (1 mark).
Moles of Ba(OH)2 = 1.13 x 10^-3 / 2 = 5.65 x 10^-4 mol, using the 1 : 2 ratio (1 mark).
Concentration = 5.65 x 10^-4 / 0.0250 = 0.0226 mol dm^-3 (1 mark).

questions.question: The diluted barium hydroxide solution (25.0 cm^3 of saturated solution made up to 250.0 cm^3) has a concentration of 0.0226 mol dm^-3. Calculate the solubility of barium hydroxide in the saturated solution in mol dm^-3 and in g dm^-3. M(Ba(OH)2) = 171.3 g mol^-1.
steps: The solution was diluted ten times (25.0 to 250.0 cm^3), so the saturated solution is 10 x 0.0226 = 0.226 mol dm^-3 (2 marks).
Mass concentration = 0.226 x 171.3 = 38.7 g dm^-3 (1 mark).

questions.question: The same method, with 25.0 cm^3 of saturated solution and 0.100 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid, is tried with magnesium hydroxide. A saturated solution of magnesium hydroxide has a concentration of about 1.1 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3. Calculate the volume of acid needed and explain why the method is unsuitable.
questions.answer: About 0.055 cm^3, which is too small to measure with a burette
steps: Moles of OH- in 25.0 cm^3 = 2 x 1.1 x 10^-4 x 0.0250 = 5.5 x 10^-6 mol (1 mark).
This is smaller than the uncertainty in a burette reading (+/- 0.05 cm^3), so the percentage uncertainty in the titre would be huge (1 mark).

questions.question: The enthalpy change of solution of lithium chloride is -37 kJ mol^-1. The lattice energy of LiCl is -848 kJ mol^-1 and the enthalpy change of hydration of Li+(g) is -519 kJ mol^-1. Calculate the enthalpy change of hydration of Cl-(g).
steps: Delta solH = -(lattice energy) + Delta hydH(Li+) + Delta hydH(Cl-) (1 mark).
Delta hydH(Cl-) = -37 - 848 + 519 = -366 kJ mol^-1 (1 mark).

questions.question: Describe a test to show that an aqueous solution contains sulfate ions. Give the reagents, the observation and an ionic equation with state symbols.
questions.answer: Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate of BaSO4 forms. Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s)
steps: Add dilute hydrochloric acid (or nitric acid) to the solution to remove carbonate and other ions that would also form precipitates
Then add barium chloride (or barium nitrate) solution and a white precipitate forms
Ionic equation: Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s)
accept: The white precipitate does not dissolve in the excess acid
Acid prevents a white precipitate of barium carbonate (or barium sulfite) forming, which would give a false positive
Barium nitrate with nitric acid is an acceptable reagent combination
Observation: colourless solution turns cloudy white

questions.question: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.200 mol dm^-3 barium chloride solution is added to an excess of aqueous sodium sulfate. The barium sulfate precipitate is filtered off, washed and dried, and its mass is 1.08 g. Calculate the maximum mass of barium sulfate that can form, and the percentage yield. M(BaSO4) = 233.4 g mol^-1.
steps: Moles of BaCl2 = 0.0250 x 0.200 = 5.00 x 10^-3 mol, and the ratio BaCl2 : BaSO4 is 1 : 1 (1 mark).
Maximum mass = 5.00 x 10^-3 x 233.4 = 1.17 g (1 mark).
Percentage yield = 1.08 / 1.167 x 100 = 92.5% (1 mark).

questions.question: The enthalpy change of solution of calcium sulfate is exothermic, about -18 kJ mol^-1, but calcium sulfate is only sparingly soluble in water. Suggest an explanation in terms of entropy changes.
questions.answer: The entropy of the system decreases because the highly charged ions order the water molecules, so the total entropy change is small or negative
steps: The process is exothermic, so the entropy change of the surroundings is positive (-Delta H / T)
Ca2+ and SO4^2- ions have high charge densities and attract water molecules strongly, so water molecules become more ordered in the hydration shells and the entropy of the system decreases
This decrease largely or completely cancels the positive entropy change of the surroundings, so the total entropy change is small or negative and little calcium sulfate dissolves
accept: Delta S surroundings is about +60 J K^-1 mol^-1 (18 000 / 298), which is outweighed by a larger negative Delta S system
Delta S total must be greater than zero for dissolving to be feasible
The two ions are each doubly charged (2+ and 2-), so more water molecules are held in an ordered arrangement than for singly charged ions

questions.question: The solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group from magnesium sulfate to barium sulfate. Explain this trend in terms of the lattice energy and the enthalpy change of hydration of the ions.
questions.answer: The hydration enthalpy of the cation becomes less exothermic by more than the lattice energy does, so the enthalpy change of solution becomes less exothermic
steps: The enthalpy change of solution = -(lattice energy) + the sum of the enthalpy changes of hydration of the ions; a less exothermic value means a less soluble sulfate
Down the group the cations get larger, so the charge density of the cation falls
The enthalpy change of hydration of the cation becomes less exothermic, as the attraction to water molecules is weaker

The lattice energy also becomes less exothermic, but by a smaller amount, because the sulfate ion is large compared with all of the cations, so the change in cation size has little effect on the ion separation
So the hydration enthalpy becomes less exothermic by more than the lattice energy does, the enthalpy change of solution becomes less exothermic (more endothermic) and the solubility decreases
accept: Mg2+ has the highest charge density, so MgSO4 has the most exothermic hydration enthalpy and is the most soluble
Barium sulfate is the least soluble sulfate in the group
Both ions in the lattice are doubly charged, so the lattice energy is large for every sulfate, but it varies little with the cation
Ionic radius of the cation increases down the group
